subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The First Electric Cars
description: A quick win: understand The First Electric Cars.

hook.text: Electric cars aren't new. In the 1890s, they were more popular than gasoline cars.

buildup.text: They were quiet, easy to start, and didn't require hand-cranking like dangerous gas engines.

discovery.text: By 1900, electric cars made up about a third of all vehicles on American roads.

twist.text: Women preferred electrics because they didn't need physical strength to start or operate.

climax.text: Thomas Edison even worked on better batteries for them, predicting electrics would dominate.

punchline.text: Edison was right—he was just a century early.

quiz.question: What share of US vehicles were electric around 1900?

details.summary: Electric cars appeared in the 1830s and 1840s, decades before gasoline automobiles, when inventors in Hungary, the Netherlands, and Scotland built crude battery-powered vehicles as scientific experiments.
details.whyItMatters: Most people assume electric cars are a recent invention. In reality, they predate gasoline cars by half a century, making the current EV revolution a return to automotive origins, not a new concept.
takeaways: Battery-powered carriages appeared in the 1830s and 1840s
They predated the first gasoline car by roughly 50 years
Early batteries were non-rechargeable and extremely heavy

faq.question: Who built the first electric car?
faq.answer: The exact first is debated. Hungarian inventor Anyos Jedlik built a small electric vehicle model in 1828. Scottish inventor Robert Anderson built a crude electric carriage around 1832. These were experimental, not practical transportation.

faq.question: Why didn't early electric cars succeed?
faq.answer: Early batteries were single-use, extremely heavy, and provided very limited range. Rechargeable lead-acid batteries did not arrive until the 1860s, and even then, energy density was far too low for practical long-distance travel.
